### Derivative rules {#sec-derivative-rules}

:::{#thm-deriv-const}
#### Constant rule

If $c$ is constant with respect to $x$, then

$$\deriv{x}c = 0$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/videos/_note-video-deriv-const.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-const-factor}
#### Constant multiple rule

If $a$ is constant with respect to $x$
and $y$ is a differentiable function of $x$, then:
$$\deriv{x}ay = a \derivf{y}{x}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/videos/_note-video-deriv-const-factor.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-polynomial}
#### Power rule

For every real number $q$ and every $x > 0$
[@wikipedia_power_rule],
the derivative of the [power](algebra.qmd#def-real-power) $x^q$ is:

$$\deriv{x}x^q = qx^{q-1}$$

When $q$ is a positive [integer](number-systems.qmd#def-integers),
the same formula holds for every real $x$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/videos/_note-video-power-rule.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-polynomial-root.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-find-slopes.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-log}

#### Derivative of natural logarithm

For every $x > 0$,
the derivative of the [natural logarithm](algebra.qmd#def-natural-log) is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dlogf{x}
&= \frac{1}{x} \\
&= x^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-log-simplify.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-exp}
#### Derivative of exponential

For every real $x$,
the derivative of the [exponential function](algebra.qmd#def-exponential-function) is:

$$\dexpf{x} = \expf{x}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-sin}
#### Derivative of sine

For every real $x$,
the derivative of the sine function is:

$$\deriv{x}\sin x = \cos x$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-cos}
#### Derivative of cosine

For every real $x$,
the derivative of the cosine function is:

$$\deriv{x}\cos x = -\sin x$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-product-rule}
#### Product rule

If $a$ and $b$ are differentiable functions of $x$
[@wikipedia_product_rule], then

$$(ab)' = ab' + ba'$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/videos/_note-video-product-rule.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-product-poly-cos.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-second-product.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-quotient-rule}
#### Quotient rule

If $a$ and $b$ are differentiable functions of $x$
[@wikipedia_quotient_rule]
and $b \neq 0$, then

$$(a/b)' = a'/b - (a/b^2)b'$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/videos/_note-video-quotient-rule.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-quotient-or-factor.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-chain-rule}
#### Chain rule

If $a$ is a differentiable function of $b$
[@wikipedia_chain_rule],
and $b$ is a differentiable function of $c$,
then $a$ is a differentiable function of $c$, and

$$\ba
\dif{a}{c} &=
\dif{a}{b} \dif{b}{c}
\\
&= \dif{b}{c} \dif{a}{b}
\ea
$$

or in Lagrange's notation (@def-derivative),
if $g$ is differentiable at $x$
and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$,
then for the [composition](functions.qmd#def-composition) $f \circ g$,
with inner function $g$ and outer function $f$:

$$(f(g(x)))' = g'(x) f'(g(x))$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-gaussian-kernel.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_thm-deriv-gaussian-kernel.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-second-gaussian-kernel.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_thm-deriv-second-gaussian-kernel.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-product-chain-composite.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-generalized-power-rule.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-deriv-log-chain}

#### Chain rule for logarithms

If $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f(x) > 0$, then

$$
\dif{}{x}\logf{f(x)} = \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}
$$

:::

::: proof
Apply @thm-chain-rule and @thm-deriv-log:

$$
\ba
\dif{}{x}\logf{f(x)}
&= f'(x) \cd \dlogf{f(x)}
&& \text{(chain rule, with } g = f \text{ and outer function } \log \text{)}
\\
&= f'(x) \cd \frac{1}{f(x)}
&& \text{(derivative of } \log \text{, valid because } f(x) > 0 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\ea
$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/videos/_note-video-chain-rule.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include mds/_subfiles/calculus-review/_exr-miller-deriv-chain-log.qmd >}}

### Linear approximation {#sec-linear-approximation}

For a differentiable function $f$ and a small step $\smallconst$,

$$f(w + \smallconst) \approx f(w) + \smallconst\,\dif{}{w}f(w)$$ {#eq-linear-approx}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-linear-approximation}
#### Linear approximation (first-order Taylor approximation)

For a function $f$ that is differentiable at $w$,
the **linear approximation** of $f$ at $w$
[@wikipedia_linear_approximation]
(also called the **first-order Taylor approximation**)
is the function of the step $\smallconst$

$$\hat{f}_w(\smallconst) = f(w) + \smallconst\,\dif{}{w}f(w)$$

so @eq-linear-approx says $f(w + \smallconst) \approx \hat{f}_w(\smallconst)$ for small $\smallconst$.
@fig-linear-approx illustrates this approximation interactively for a quadratic function.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-linear-approx-affine}
#### The "linear" approximation is affine

The linear approximation $\hat{f}_w$ (@def-linear-approximation)
is an [affine function](algebra.qmd#def-affine-function) of the step $\smallconst$:
its slope is $\dif{}{w}f(w)$ and its intercept is $f(w)$.
It is [linear](algebra.qmd#def-linear-function) in $\smallconst$ only when $f(w) = 0$.
The name "linear approximation" uses "linear" in the looser sense of elementary algebra
([remark](algebra.qmd#rem-linear-function-terminology)).
@boyd2018vmls, section 2.2, treats the first-order Taylor approximation
as an affine function for functions of several variables as well.

:::
